summary:
Afghanistan under the Taliban is the most hostile environment on this map for a transgender person. No legal protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity existed before the 2021 takeover and none exists after it, according to the EUAA COI Report of February 2026. The Taliban's Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice Law of 31 July 2024, in its Article 22, obliges the regime's overseers to prevent listed evils including lesbianism and homosexuality "even if with one's own spouse", placing same-sex conduct under continuous moral surveillance alongside adultery and gambling.

Criminalisation is layered. The Human Dignity Trust country profile, updated 19 January 2026, records that Afghanistan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women: Penal Code 2017 provisions on "sodomy" and "inciting sodomy" carry up to two years' imprisonment, while the Code's Sharia-reference clause permits the death penalty for same-sex activity. Amnesty International, cited in the EUAA COI Report, states that same-sex relations are punishable by death, and reporting from October 2021 records the same conclusion as applied by the ruling movement.

Enforcement has intensified and is public. OHCHR reported in March 2026 that UN human-rights experts condemned a surge in corporal punishment, with at least 1,110 people flogged during 2025 alone, nearly double the 2024 figure, and warned that women, girls and LGBT+ people face heightened punishment for moral crimes including adultery, illicit relationships and sodomy. OutRight International reported in February 2023, from interviews conducted with LGBTIQ Afghans still in the country in September and October 2022, that Taliban security officials pursue gay men and trans women more systematically than in the early months of rule, using physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations; the Taliban Supreme Court has confirmed such punishments on social media.

Detention is documented as abusive. CNN reported in November 2024 first-person accounts of arbitrary detention, beatings and sexual abuse in Taliban custody as the crackdown intensified. The Human Rights Watch and OutRight report of 26 January 2022, based on 60 interviews, found that Taliban members and their supporters attack, threaten and expel LGBT people from their homes, that abuse by family, neighbours and partners surged after the takeover, and that many went into hiding or fled. Reporting from Kabul in October 2021 documented street attacks on men coded as gay, with victims changing their clothing and confining themselves indoors.

Visibly transgender people carry the gravest risk. The JURIST feature of 8 November 2024, drawing on the Rainbow Organization of Afghanistan formed by Afghan LGBTQ refugees in Bremen, reports systematic persecution after August 2021 and notes that even the post-2001 constitution provided no protective framework. Transgender residents describe years of hiding in windowless rooms. A discovered trans visitor would be processed by the same apparatus as local LGBTIQ people: moral-police surveillance under the 2024 law, arbitrary detention, corporal punishment, and abuse in custody, with no legal recognition, no protection machinery, and no consular recourse that operates for LGBTIQ detainees.
tangentialFactors:
The European Union Agency for Asylum treats LGBTIQ Afghans, in its Country Guidance section 3.17, as persons perceived to transgress religious and social norms, grouped with minors without support networks and persons facing the death penalty. That classification, in guidance current as of May 2024, is the asylum-framework basis for assessing Afghan LGBTIQ protection claims in the EU, and it functions as an official external finding that persecution is well founded rather than a private judgement.

The UN warning of March 2026 places LGBT+ people within a broader punitive turn: the 1,110 floggings recorded in 2025 were not confined to sexual offences, but the experts specifically flagged moral-crime categories where LGBT+ people are exposed. A trans visitor therefore enters a jurisdiction where public corporal punishment has become routine state practice, not an exceptional measure reserved for a narrow class of case.

Rainbow symbolism and organised advocacy operate only in exile. The Rainbow Organization of Afghanistan was formed by Afghan LGBTQ refugees in Bremen, Germany, and the documented networks of support for people who fled post-August 2021 are diaspora-based. Nothing comparable is reported as functioning inside the country.
localsOnly:
Residents found in same-sex conduct face a two-track penalty structure. The Penal Code 2017 provisions on sodomy and inciting sodomy carry up to two years, while the same Code's Sharia-reference clause allows the death penalty; the Supreme Court has publicly confirmed punishments of the latter kind on social media, and public flogging is among the documented sentences.

Article 22 of the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice Law places an affirmative duty on the overseer to prevent lesbianism and homosexuality, including conduct within marriage, which converts private life into an enforceable offence and gives the virtue police grounds to enter homes and interrogate residents. The 2022 and 2023 interview-based reports record house-to-house searches, forced confessions, and beatings as reported practice.

Abuse is not limited to state actors. Family, neighbour and partner violence rose sharply after August 2021, and Taliban members and supporters have expelled LGBT people from their homes. Transgender residents report hiding in windowless rooms for years, and visibly transgender individuals are described as facing the gravest risks, including exploitation and violence, above those faced by gay men and lesbians.
outOfScopeNotes:
The relative weight of the Penal Code's two-year maximum against the Sharia-reference death penalty in actual sentencing is not resolved in the inventory; the sources state both provisions without indicating which is applied in a given case, and no conviction-level data is available here.

No sourced material addresses how a trans visitor's passport gender marker is read at entry, whether visa applications or arrival screening ask questions that would disclose gender history, or what consular assistance a foreign mission would attempt for a detained dual-national or foreign trans person. The claim of no consular recourse rests on the general absence of protection machinery rather than on a documented consular case.

The inventory does not establish whether the 2024 Morality Law's provisions apply with identical force in every province, nor does it document enforcement against foreign nationals specifically; all first-person accounts sourced here concern Afghan residents or those who fled.

Reporting on detention abuse in November 2024 and on the flogging totals in March 2026 carries dates but no figures for LGBT-specific detentions, so the scale of trans detainees remains unquantified.
